CELL BIOLOGY LABORATORY NEFISSA HAMOUD HOSPITAL
The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ of abdominal location placed on the blood path located at the level of the left hypochondrium.
The spleen appears around the 5th week of embryonic development.
Of exclusively mesenchymal origin, its outline is built in the posterior or dorsal midgut following a local proliferation of the coelomic layer.
The spleen offers to describe three types of constituents:
The connective elements, forming the fibro-elastic and muscular framework.
The splenic pulp with its two aspects: white pulp and red pulp.
The fibrous skeleton of the spleen includes:
-a peripheral envelope capsule formed of collagen fibers, elastic fibers and smooth muscle fibers.

-partitions coming from the deep face of the capsule incompletely delimiting lobes whose parenchyma is subdivided into lobules by secondary trabeculae, these trabeculae continue in a reticular framework which supports the splenic pulp.

Made up of lymphoid tissue developed around the arteries of the splenic pulp presenting visible swellings: the MALPIGHI corpuscles which are lymphoid nodules with a whitish appearance with a clear germinal center and a capillary system originating from the corpuscular artery.
-T lymphocytes from the deep layer of the periarterial sheath.
-B lymphocytes of the superficial layer of the periarterial sheath, organized into primary nodules or secondary nodules each having a germinal center.
Lymphocytes enter and exit the periarterial lymphoid sheath through the blood capillaries of the central arteriole located in the marginal zone separating the lymphoid tissue from the red pulp.
The MALPIGHI corpuscles of the splenic white pulp examined in mo at high magnification are nodules crossed by an arteriole.
1- on the topographic level: the pulpal arterioles give rise to the corpuscular arterioles in the MALPIGHI corpuscle, the latter divide into terminal penicillated arterioles.
2-morphologically: the terminal end of the penicillated arterioles is provided with a contractile device: the SCHWEIGER-SEIDEL cover.
Sphincter formations characterize the capillary segments of the venous network.

The majority of splenic T cells reside in the non-nodular portion of the periarterial sheath immediately surrounding the central arteriole. Macrophages tend to congregate in the marginal zone between the white and red pulp, and at this level they begin to process red blood cells for possible phagocytosis.

The spleen filters and “cleans” the blood in the same way that lymph nodes filter lymph.
-Hemolytic organ where the destruction of aged red blood cells is ensured.
-Lymphoid organ ensuring the recognition and capture of ATG circulating in the blood and triggering the differentiation of immunocompetent cells
